title: How do you structure your answer in a case interview?
description: The most heavily weighted skill. How to build a MECE structure for any problem, and why you must say where you would start.
hook: Structuring is the moment most people dread: you are asked how you would approach the problem, and your mind goes blank or fills with a framework you half remember. This guide shows a simpler way. You break the problem into a few parts that do not overlap, say where you would start, and explain why. It is a skill, not a talent, and it improves quickly with practice.
body:
In this guide

  • What a structure is for
  • MECE: no overlaps, no gaps
  • Make it specific to this client
  • Always finish with a hypothesis
  • A worked example
  • What to remember
  • Check yourself

What a structure is for

A structure is your plan for solving the case, drawn as an issue tree: the question at the top, 3-4 big areas underneath, and the specific things you'd check under each. It tells the interviewer you have a plan, and it tells you what to look at next when you get lost.

MECE: no overlaps, no gaps

MECE stands for mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive. In plain words: your buckets shouldn't overlap, and together they should cover everything big. "Revenue" and "costs" are MECE for profit. "Marketing" and "customers" overlap.

Two ways to build MECE buckets:

  • By factors: split the thing into its drivers. Profit = revenue - costs; revenue = volume × price. Best for "why" questions.
  • By steps: a sequence of questions. Is the market attractive? Can we win? Do the economics work? How would we enter? Best for "should we" questions.

Make it specific to this client

The most common feedback interviewers give is "too generic". A structure that would fit any company is a framework recited from a book. Tailor each branch: for a coffee chain, revenue isn't just "volume × price", it's in-store orders × in-store ticket, plus delivery orders × delivery ticket. That one change shows you're thinking about this business.

Always finish with a hypothesis

After presenting your structure, say which branch you think holds the answer and why, then ask for the data to test it: "Revenue is roughly flat, so I suspect a cost has grown. Delivery launched in this period, so I'd start with the cost of delivery orders. Do we have a cost breakdown?" This turns you from someone listing areas into someone solving the problem. Never end with "where would you like me to start?"

See it in action: One prompt, two structures

Prompt: A hotel group is considering launching a budget brand. Should it?

Generic: Market / Competition / Customers / Company / Finances (overlapping, could be any company).

Tailored (drawn below): each branch is a question about this hotel group. Hypothesis: whether the new brand steals guests from our existing hotels is the deciding factor, because our mid-range hotels sit in the same cities.

What to remember

  • 3-4 buckets, MECE, specific to this client.
  • Factors for "why" questions; steps for "should we" questions.
  • Always end with where you’d start, and why.

Check yourself

Have a go at each one before you open the answer. Getting some wrong is how it sticks.

1. Which pair of buckets is MECE for "why did profit fall"?

  • Marketing and customers
  • Revenue and costs
  • Competitors and pricing
Show the answer

Revenue and costs. Profit = revenue - costs. Every cause sits in one or the other.

2. What should you say right after presenting your structure?

  • "Where would you like me to start?"
  • Which branch you think matters most, and why
  • A summary of the prompt
Show the answer

Which branch you think matters most, and why. Stating a hypothesis shows you’re solving the problem, not just organising it.

3. A "should we enter this market" question is usually best structured by...

  • Factors (drivers)
  • Steps (a sequence of questions)
  • The 4Ps of marketing
Show the answer

Steps (a sequence of questions). Attractiveness → can we win → economics → how to enter is a natural sequence.

Try it now

A national railway’s passenger complaints have doubled in a year. Draw a structure with 3-4 buckets, then write one sentence saying where you’d start and why.

Give yourself 2 minutes, out loud if you can. Speaking it, rather than thinking it, is what builds the skill.

Show a strong answer

Buckets: (1) More passengers or easier ways to complain: has volume or the complaints channel changed? (2) Service: punctuality, cancellations, crowding. (3) Experience: stations, staff, ticketing, information. (4) Expectations: fares or promises that changed. Hypothesis: "Complaints doubling in one year suggests a sudden change, so I’d first check whether a new app made complaining easier, then look at punctuality."
outro: You do not have to get all of this right at once. Pick one thing from this guide to focus on in your next practice case. This guide is lesson 3 of the free PrepForCase course, where you can do the exercise and quiz and track your progress.
